newsitem.title: UK: British forces seal off Catholic zone after bomb.
newsitem.headline: British forces seal off Catholic zone after bomb.

text.p: British forces sealed off part of an Irish nationalist area in West Belfast on Thursday after an explosion shook patrolling soldiers and police.
Police said no-one had been seriously hurt and a number of people had been arrested in a follow-up security operation.
The spokesman said that "some sort of device was detonated" shortly after 1300 GMT in the heart of Ballymurphy, a sprawling housing estate of Catholics who oppose British rule in Northern Ireland.
No organisation claimed responsibility for the blast but security sources said it might be the work of Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas fighting to end British rule.
"There was a joint police and army patrol in the area at the time. No ambulance has been tasked and no-one has been seriously hurt," a police spokesman said.
Security sources said army bomb disposal officers were on their way to the area, which had been cordoned of as a precaution.

IRA guerrillas have killed two British soldiers in bomb and sniper attacks in the province since last October. They abandoned a 17-month ceasefire in February 1996, launching a series of bomb attack on the British mainland before escalating hostilities in Northern Ireland.
Britain says that Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, will not be allowed to join in peace talks until the guerrillas abandon violence.
IRA attacks have shattered a delicate peace process in Northern Ireland and shaken a truce by Protestant guerrillas loyal to Britain.
A pro-British politician blamed Protestant guerrillas on Thursday for a bomb near a Sinn Fein office in the Irish Republic last Monday but said it did not mark the end of the "Loyalist" truce.

David Ervine, a leader of the political arm of the banned Loyalist Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF), said he did not know which group left the device, which failed to explode, but added: "I am fairly certain in my own mind that it was the work of Loyalism."

Irish Republic police confirmed on Wednesday that the bomb in Monaghan town contained commercial explosive that security analysts say was used in UVF bombs before the illegal Combined Loyalist Military Command called its truce in October 1994.
Progressive Unionist Party chief Ervine told Reuters: "I am assured absolutely that the CLMC ceasefire is intact."
The CLMC groups the UVF and three other outlawed groups that have killed Irish nationalists in retaliation for the IRA's campaign to merge the largely Protestant region with Catholic Ireland.

PUP politicians, who have seats in fraught multi-party peace talks because UVF fighters have stuck to their truce, say Loyalists must shun violence and put their faith in negotiations to maintain the union of Northern Ireland with Britain.
British security forces blame Loyalist hardliners for three attacks on Catholics in Northern Ireland since December.
The Monaghan bomb was the first suspected Loyalist attack in the Irish Republic since before the CLMC ceasefire.
